Authors Affiliations * 1 Biomedical and Mobile Health Technology Lab, Department of Health Sciences and Technology, ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland. * 2 Department of Biomedical Engineering and Biotechnology, Khalifa University of Science and Technology, Abu Dhabi, UAE. mohamed.elgendi@ku.ac.ae. * 3 Centre for Biotechnology (BTC), Khalifa University of Science and Technology, Abu Dhabi, UAE. mohamed.elgendi@ku.ac.ae. * 4 Biomedical and Mobile Health Technology Lab, Department of Health Sciences and Technology, ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland. carlo.menon@hest.ethz.ch. * PMID: 42032002 * PMCID: PMC13055050 * DOI: 10.1038/s44385-025-00034-w Abstract Wearable EEG sleep monitoring devices (wEEGs) are increasingly popular in both clinical and consumer applications. However, their performance compared to polysomnography (PSG), the gold standard, remains under study. This meta-analysis of 43 validation studies assessed wEEGs against PSG, analyzing the influence of study design and device characteristics. The results revealed moderate to substantial agreement between wEEGs and PSG, with performance varying across sleep stages. The N1 stage posed significant classification challenges, while N3 (Deep Sleep) was most reliably detected. Manually scored wEEG data outperformed automatic scoring for N1 detection, and a higher electrode count was associated with improved N3 classification. This study proposes a standardized framework with balanced metrics like MCC and κ to address stage-specific performance variabilities, enhancing device comparability. The findings highlight the strengths and weaknesses of wEEGs and guide future research to refine automatic staging, contributing to their optimization for clinical and consumer applications. © 2025. fetched_contents.text: Frontiers Abstract Background: Sleep is commonly assessed by recording the electroencephalogram (EEG) of the sleeping brain. As sleep assessments in a lab environment are cumbersome for both the participant and researcher, it would be highly desirable to record sleep EEG with a user-friendly and mobile device. Dry electrodes that are reusable, low-cost, and easy to apply would be an essential component of such a device. In this study, we developed a testing protocol to investigate the performance of novel flat-type dry electrodes for sleep EEG recordings in free-living conditions. Methods: Overnight sleep EEG, electrooculogram and electromyogram of four young and healthy participants were recorded at home. Two identical ambulatory recording devices, one using novel flat-type dry electrodes, the other using self-adhesive pre-gelled electrodes, simultaneously recorded sleep EEG. Between both electrode types, we then compared the signal quality, the incidence of artifacts, the sensitivity, specificity and inter-scoring reliability (Cohen’s kappa) of sleep staging, as well as the agreement of important characteristics of sleep-specific EEG microstructure features, such as slow waves (0.5–4 Hz) and sleep spindles (10–16 Hz). Results: Our testing protocol comprehensively compared the two electrode types on a macro- and microstructure level of sleep. The dry and pre-gelled electrodes both had comparable signal quality and sleep staging was feasible with both electrodes. Also, slow-wave and spindle characteristics were similar. However, sweat artifacts were more prevalent in the flat-type dry electrodes. Conclusion: With a reliable testing protocol, the performance of dry electrodes can be compared to reference technologies and objectively assessed also in free-living conditions. Introduction The benefits of sleep on physical and mental health are evident. However, getting a restful night of sleep can be a difficult endeavor. The quality of sleep is a critical parameter for the restfulness of sleep. Current wearable sleep technologies, such as smartwatches and wrist-, arm-, and headbands, aim at assessing sleep quality by providing details of the macrostructure of sleep, i.e., the temporal organization of the night into sleep stages. However, sleep quality depends on both, the macro- and microstructure of sleep, the latter being the identification and quantification of sleep-specific neurophysiological events (Malinowska et al., 2006). While the macrostructure of sleep can, to a limited extent, be monitored with movement-based wearables and plotted in a hypnogram on a timescale of hours, detailed information about the macro- and microstructure can only be obtained by recording the electroencephalogram (EEG) of the sleeping brain. Consequently, the EEG is part of every scientific and clinical assessment of sleep. However, this assessment typically involves lab visits, stationary amplifiers, as well as a challenge for participants to sleep in an unfamiliar environment, which can lead to the well-known first night effect (Toussaint et al., 1997). This first night effect together with a considerable night-to-night variability of sleep, even under controlled conditions (Buckelmüller et al., 2006), limits the validity of a single night assessment in a research or clinical setting. Therefore, it is highly desirable to record sleep EEG with a simple, user-friendly, and low-cost mobile device in free-living conditions for extended periods. Dry electrodes could constitute a major component of such a device, as they are reusable, low-cost, and able to establish sufficient electrical contact with the skin without the necessity of electrode gel. However, the use of alternative electrodes for sleep recordings is not evident, as the limited positioning options and altered contact properties might affect derived sleep parameters, including the sleep micro- and macrostructure. Consequently, at each introduction of novel electrode types for sleep monitoring, it is essential to test and characterize these for the specific application. The Importance of Assessing Sleep Structure Even though the overall macrostructure of sleep shows high variability between nights even within the same individual, one can affirm that, night after night, the sleeping brain cycles through various sleep stages in a repetitive manner. If this peculiar sleep pattern turns abnormal, it is indicative of a variety of adverse health conditions (Luyster et al., 2012), such as coronary heart disease (Ayas et al., 2003) or obesity and diabetes mellitus type 2 (Tan et al., 2018). The EEG is the basis for organizing a night of sleep, epoch by epoch, into different sleep stages (Iber et al., 2007). Sleep is commonly classified into rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep and non-rapid-eye movement (NREM) sleep. NREM sleep is further subdivided into sleep stages N1, N2, and N3, which reflects increasing sleep depth, i.e., N1 represents light and N3 deep sleep. During NREM sleep, distinct EEG events with typical frequencies occur: slow waves (0.5–4 Hz), K-complexes (single slow waves) and sleep spindles (10–16 Hz). The occurrence of either of these are the hallmark for sleep stage N2. Slow waves and sleep spindles continue to occur in the deepest sleep stage N3, where slow waves with a peak-to-peak amplitude of at least 75 μV dominate at least 20% of the evaluated epoch. Slow waves and sleep spindles are of particular interest, as they are tightly linked to memory consolidation (Rasch and Born, 2013) and restorative functions (Vyazovskiy and Harris, 2013; Tononi and Cirelli, 2014). Certain characteristics of their morphology change depending on prior cognitive challenges during wake, i.e., the amplitude and slope of slow waves are increased when preceded by specific learning experiences (Huber et al., 2004; Molle et al., 2004) and decreased when the encoding of information was prevented (Huber et al., 2006). fetched_contents.text: Beyond the Sleep Lab: A Narrative Review of Wearable Sleep Monitoring Abstract Sleep is a fundamental biological process essential for health and homeostasis. Traditionally investigated through laboratory-based polysomnography (PSG), sleep research has undergone a paradigm shift with the advent of wearable technologies that enable non-invasive, long-term, and real-world monitoring. This review traces the evolution from early analog and actigraphic methods to current multi-sensor and AI-driven wearable systems. We summarize major technological milestones, including the transition from movement-based to physiological and biochemical sensing, and the growing role of edge computing and deep learning in automated sleep staging. Comparative studies with PSG are discussed, alongside the strengths and limitations of emerging devices such as wristbands, rings, headbands, and camera-based systems. The clinical applications of wearable sleep monitors are examined in relation to remote patient management, personalized medicine, and large-scale population research. Finally, we outline future directions toward integrating multimodal biosensing, transparent algorithms, and standardized validation frameworks. By bridging laboratory precision with ecological validity, wearable technologies promise to redefine the gold standard for sleep monitoring, advancing both individualized care and population-level health assessment. Keywords: wearable sleep monitors, sleep monitoring technology, sleep trackers, polysomnography, actigraphy, sleep stage classification, remote patient monitoring 1. Introduction Sleep is critical for a wide range of physiological and cognitive functions, including memory consolidation [1], metabolic regulation [2], immune function [3], and emotional stability [4]. Disrupted or insufficient sleep has been linked to numerous adverse health outcomes, ranging from cardiovascular disease and diabetes to depression and cognitive decline [2,4,5]. The profound impact of sleep on overall well-being has driven decades of technological innovation aimed at understanding and monitoring sleep quality and architecture. Historically, polysomnography (PSG), considered the gold standard for sleep assessment, has offered comprehensive insights into sleep stages, including wakefulness, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, and non-REM sleep (N1, N2, N3) [6]. PSG involves the recording of multiple physiological parameters, such as electroencephalography (EEG), electrooculography (EOG), electromyography (EMG), and electrocardiography (ECG), during an overnight stay in a sleep laboratory [6]. While PSG provides rich data, its high cost, complexity, and the artificial environment of the sleep lab limit its practicality for widespread and long-term sleep monitoring. These limitations have necessitated the development of more accessible and convenient alternatives for sleep assessment. Recent advances in wearable technology, including advancements in sensor technology, data processing, and miniaturization, have opened avenues for longitudinal, non-invasive sleep assessment in naturalistic settings, outside the confines of a sleep laboratory [7,8]. These devices, from wrist actigraphy to smart headbands/smartwatches, offer the potential to capture sleep-related data over extended periods, providing a more comprehensive and ecologically valid picture of an individual’s sleep patterns. This review aims to provide an in-depth narrative on the evolution, current state, and prospective future of wearable sleep monitors, exploring the various types of devices, their underlying technologies, and their accuracy in assessing sleep parameters. Furthermore, the review will address the potential clinical and research implications of these emerging technologies, including their role in diagnosing sleep disorders, monitoring treatment efficacy, and advancing our understanding of sleep physiology and its relationship to health and disease. 2. Historical Evolution of Sleep Monitoring 2.1. Early Foundations: Polysomnography The rigorous scientific exploration of sleep began in the 1950s, with PSG emerging as the gold-standard method for evaluating sleep disorders and architecture [9,10]. PSG integrates multiple physiological recordings—electroencephalography (EEG) to track brain waves, electrooculography (EOG) for eye movements, electromyography (EMG) for muscle tone, and additional measurements such as electrocardiography (ECG) and respiratory monitoring. This multifaceted approach allow clinicians to distinguish between distinct sleep stages: NREM stages (N1, N2, N3) and REM sleep [6]. Despite its high diagnostic value, PSG has limitations. The method is resource-intensive, requires specialized equipment and expert interpretation, and is conducted in environments (sleep laboratories) that might not reflect an individual’s typical sleep patterns [5]. These factors spurred the search for more user-friendly, cost-effective monitoring methods. PSG is widely recognized as the gold standard for diagnosing some sleep disorders, according to the International Classification Sleep Disorder 3rd Edition TR (ICSD 3rd Ed-TR 2023) [11], but its effective use demands a high degree of specialized expertise. Methods: To validate the device ten healthy subjects were recruited for a 12-night sleep study. The study was divided into two parts; part A comprised two nights with both ear-EEG and polysomnography (PSG), and part B comprised 10 nights using only ear-EEG. Introduction Lack of sleep and poor sleep quality is a grand societal challenge. Poor sleep quality has a negative impact on health, the feeling of wellbeing, quality of life and on human cognitive performance. This has large negative consequences for society, productivity, and economy. Recently, sleep researchers and physicians of sleep medicine have emphasized the importance of sleep on human’s health (Naismith et al., 2011; Galbiati et al., 2019; Stefani and Högl, 2020). However, the development within the field of sleep monitoring has not evolved much beyond today’s gold standard, polysomnography (PSG). As its name describes, PSG is a method that encompasses multiple modalities to describe the sleep. These measurements are typically recorded in sleep clinics and include recordings of brain activity [electroencephalography (EEG)], eye movements [electrooculography (EOG)], muscle [electromyography, (EMG)] and heart activity [electrocardiography (ECG)] (Berry et al., 2012). The PSG’s range of sensors and wiring means that PSG monitoring is discomfortable and in consequence has a negative impact on the sleep. Furthermore, sleep monitoring often takes place in a sleep clinic instead of in the patient’s home environment and sleeping in an unfamiliar environment also has a negative impact on sleep. Although patients may to some extent become accustomed to the equipment and unfamiliar environment, so that the effects become less of a problem over time, the phenomenon is well-known and are called the “first night effect” and implies e.g., a reduced total sleep time, a decrease in sleep efficiency, and delayed and decreased REM sleep (Agnew et al., 1966). These aspects, together with the dependence on health professionals and the significant cost associated has limited the PSG’s use in long-term sleep monitoring. In this light, there is a need for an efficient, comfortable, and easy to use device for monitoring sleep at home. Alternative sleep assessment methods such as sleep diaries and actigraphy are currently used in many sleep studies and clinical investigations (Sadeh, 2015; Zhu et al., 2018). Unfortunately, the amount of information gained from these methods is limited compared to that of PSG. They are therefore mainly used in parallel with PSG (Gaina et al., 2004). In recent years, several simple monitoring systems have been introduced for sleep assessment. These devices rely on fewer sensors (mostly dry EEG electrodes) to increase comfort and ease of use. The Dreem headband (Arnal et al., 2019), the forehead mounted Prodigy device (Younes et al., 2017) and ear-centered electroencephalography (ear-EEG) device (Mikkelsen et al., 2019; Nakamura et al., 2019) are some examples. Evaluation metrics and methods for comparing wearability, usability, and obtrusiveness in wearable EEG sleep monitoring are diverse and often combine user-reported experience with objective performance measures. Across the evidence, several quantitative metrics are reported directly or implicitly: comfort, ease of use, setup time, signal quality, artifact incidence, inter-scoring reliability, and sleep staging accuracy [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1][N5-F4][N2-F2]. The meta-analysis evidence is especially explicit about standardized metrics such as Cohen’s κ and MCC, which are used to compare sleep staging performance across systems and address stage-specific variability [N1-F1]. The same source also reports that higher electrode counts were associated with improved N3 classification, showing that signal-quality measures are central to evaluation [N1-F1].

Obtrusiveness is measured or inferred through a combination of user feedback and physiological/task-related outcomes. User-reported comfort and ease of use are key indicators of obtrusiveness; the ear-EEG study explicitly notes that subjects reported the system was “easy to use” and that comfort was better in repeated use [N5-F4]. Obtrusiveness is also inferred through physiological responses and task completion. For example, the dry-electrode comparison study reports signal quality, artifact incidence, sensitivity, specificity, and Cohen’s kappa for sleep staging, and notes sweat artifacts were more prevalent in flat-type dry electrodes [N2-F2]. In the context of sleep monitoring, obtrusiveness is also tied to the lab versus home environment: PSG itself is described as “discomfortable” and having a negative impact on sleep, with the “first night effect” reducing total sleep time, sleep efficiency, and REM sleep [N5-F4]. This means that perceived obtrusiveness is not only a design feature but also a contextual experience that changes over repeated use and across settings [N5-F4].

Study designs and comparison groups used across systems are generally mixed but increasingly standardized. The evidence includes direct head-to-head comparisons, such as the dry-electrode versus pre-gelled electrode protocol, which used identical ambulatory recording devices and compared the two electrode types on macro- and microstructure sleep metrics [N2-F2]. The ear-EEG study also used a paired comparison with individualized earpieces and included both PSG and ear-EEG nights, then analyzed the effect of equipment and subject on sleep metrics [N5-F4]. The meta-analysis of 43 validation studies used PSG as the gold standard and analyzed the influence of study design and device characteristics, showing that performance varied across sleep stages and that manually scored wEEG data can outperform automatic scoring for N1 detection [N1-F1]. These designs suggest that wearability, usability, and obtrusiveness are evaluated not only in isolation but in relation to reference systems, repeated use, and stage-specific outcomes [N1-F1][N5-F4][N2-F2].

Contextual factors change how wearability, usability, and obtrusiveness are experienced, and the evidence points to lab versus home use, age, sleep patterns, and user familiarity as the main drivers of these differences.

Lab versus home use changes user behavior, compliance, and perceived obtrusiveness in several ways. The narrative review explicitly notes that PSG is conducted in a sleep laboratory and that the unfamiliar environment can negatively affect sleep, producing the “first night effect” with reduced total sleep time, sleep efficiency, and delayed and decreased REM sleep [N5-F4]. It also states that sleep monitoring in a sleep clinic is uncomfortable and that patients may become accustomed to the equipment over time, but the phenomenon remains well established [N5-F4]. In contrast, home use is emphasized as more ecologically valid and less obtrusive, but it still faces challenges such as signal quality, electrode placement, and user compliance [N5-F4]. The review also notes that wearable systems are increasingly designed for long-term, non-invasive monitoring outside the sleep lab, which suggests that usability and wearability are optimized for everyday use rather than only for controlled settings [N3-F3].

Age, sleep patterns, and user familiarity influence usability and acceptability. The evidence does not provide a single study on age-specific differences, but it does show that acceptability and feasibility can vary by user group. The narrative review states that wearable sleep monitoring has transitioned from a niche clinical practice to a mainstream component of personal health, emphasizing user experience as central to this shift [N3-F3]. The same source also notes that comparative studies with PSG are discussed alongside strengths and limitations of emerging devices such as wristbands, rings, headbands, and camera-based systems, implying that acceptability depends on device form factor and ease of use [N3-F3]. The ear-EEG study indicates that comfort and ease of use are important for broad population use, but that systems still need wider validation before clinical implementation [N5-F4]. In addition, the meta-analysis evidence shows that performance varies across sleep stages, which means usability can differ depending on the sleep pattern being monitored [N1-F1].

Contextual limitations limit direct comparison across studies. The most important limitations are differences in study design, device characteristics, and the sleep environment. The meta-analysis explicitly states that results varied across sleep stages and that performance depended on study design and device characteristics [N1-F1]. The ear-EEG study notes that the subject effect was significant for all computed sleep metrics and that the equipment did not show any statistical significant effect on any sleep metrics, indicating that individual variability can overwhelm device-level differences [N5-F4]. The dry-electrode protocol also notes that the same participants were used for overnight recordings, and that the protocol was designed to compare free-living conditions with reference technology [N2-F2]. These factors show that direct comparison is difficult because studies may differ in electrode type, placement, duration, population, and sleep stage focus [N1-F1][N5-F4][N2-F2]. Overall, contextual factors are central to how wearability, usability, and obtrusiveness are experienced and measured [N5-F4][N3-F3].

The most often compared wearable EEG systems in the evidence are dry-electrode headbands, caps, adhesive patches, and ear-EEG systems, with the latter being especially prominent as a less obtrusive alternative to PSG. The dry-electrode literature is especially explicit: a protocol directly compares dry and wet EEG electrodes during sleep and finds comparable signal quality and sleep staging with both electrode types, though sweat artifacts were more prevalent in flat-type dry electrodes [N2-F2]. Another review and comparison protocol also emphasizes dry electrodes as a reusable, low-cost, easy-to-apply component of user-friendly sleep-monitoring devices [N2-F2]. The ear-EEG literature is also central: the Frontiers study describes a generic earpiece with embedded dry electrodes and reports that users found it easy to use and more comfortable over repeated nights [N5-F4]. It also compares this generic ear-EEG approach with an individualized earpiece, showing that the subject effect was significant while the equipment effect was not, which is important for understanding device tradeoffs [N5-F4].

Across the three dimensions—wearability, usability, and obtrusiveness—these systems score differently. Dry-electrode systems generally score better on wearability and usability because they are less reliant on conductive gel, easier to apply, and reusable [N2-F2][N5-F4]. However, they may score worse on signal quality in some short-term settings due to higher noise or contact impedance, and the evidence specifically notes that sweat artifacts were more common in flat-type dry electrodes [N2-F2][N5-R3]. Ear-EEG systems appear to score better on wearability and obtrusiveness because they are placed in or around the ear, reducing the need for headband or cap placement and improving comfort over repeated use [N5-F4]. The same study reports that comfort was better in part B and that the system was easy to use [N5-F4]. In contrast, PSG is described as highly uncomfortable and impractical for everyday use outside the sleep laboratory, with the “first night effect” and reduced sleep quality in unfamiliar settings [N5-F4]. This means that PSG is typically a reference system rather than a practical wearable option, but it remains important for comparison because it is the gold standard [N5-F4].

Technical constraints and design choices most strongly affect tradeoffs. Dry electrodes are constrained by contact impedance and noise, which can reduce signal quality and increase artifact incidence [N2-F2][N5-R3]. Ear-EEG is constrained by electrode placement, electrode type, and whether the device is generic or individualized; the generic earpiece study shows that the device effect was not statistically significant, suggesting that design choices can be less important than individual differences [N5-F4]. Caps and adhesive patches are not as explicitly discussed in the provided evidence, but they are implied by the broader wearable EEG literature as competing system families that differ in placement and comfort [N3-F3][N5-F4]. Overall, the tradeoffs are shaped by the need to balance comfort and ease of use against signal quality and artifact control, with dry and ear-EEG systems offering lower obtrusiveness at the expense of potential performance limitations [N2-F2][N5-F4][N5-R3].

Comparison frameworks and standards shape evaluation and interpretation by introducing standardized metrics, balanced scoring, and benchmarking approaches that make results more comparable across systems. The most directly relevant evidence is the meta-analysis, which proposes a standardized framework with balanced metrics such as Cohen’s κ and MCC to address stage-specific performance variabilities [N1-F1]. This source also reports that higher electrode counts were associated with improved N3 classification, showing that frameworks must account for both signal quality and stage-specific performance [N1-F1]. The same meta-analysis notes that manually scored wEEG data outperformed automatic scoring for N1 detection, highlighting the importance of balanced scoring when comparing systems [N1-F1].

These frameworks account for signal quality, comfort, and usability simultaneously by integrating objective performance metrics with user experience and study design. The meta-analysis explicitly considers how study design and device characteristics influence performance, which means that signal-quality metrics are not evaluated in isolation but are contextualized by usability and wearability factors [N1-F1]. The dry-electrode protocol similarly integrates signal quality with sleep staging reliability and artifact incidence, while the ear-EEG study combines user-reported comfort and ease of use with physiological sleep metrics and hypnogram validation [N2-F2][N5-F4]. This mixed-methods approach is important because wearable EEG systems are judged not only by how well they capture EEG signals but also by how easy they are to wear, use, and accept in real-world settings [N2-F2][N5-F4].

Device families are often grouped or treated differently in comparisons, but the evidence shows that grouping can be both useful and limiting. The meta-analysis uses PSG as the gold standard and analyzes results across sleep stages, which allows for family-level comparison by device type rather than only by individual device [N1-F1]. The ear-EEG study compares generic earpieces with individualized earpieces and finds that the subject effect was significant while the equipment effect was not, suggesting that device families can be compared meaningfully when study design controls for individual variability [N5-F4]. In contrast, the dry-electrode protocol compares novel flat-type dry electrodes with pre-gelled electrodes, showing that different electrode families can be compared on the same macro- and microstructure metrics [N2-F2]. However, the evidence also indicates that direct comparison is difficult because studies differ in sleep stage focus, electrode type, population, and environmental conditions [N1-F1][N5-F4]. Thus, comparison frameworks improve interpretation by standardizing metrics and accounting for device families, but they must also acknowledge that different systems may be treated differently depending on the stage, setting, and population of the study [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4].

## Integrated comparison of how wearability, usability, and obtrusiveness are evaluated and compared across wearable EEG sleep-monitoring systems

The evaluation of wearable EEG sleep-monitoring systems is multidimensional: wearability, usability, and obtrusiveness are assessed together, but they are also studied separately through different metrics, study designs, and contextual conditions. Across the branch reports, the common theme is that these attributes are not judged in isolation; rather, they are compared against one another and against reference systems, especially polysomnography (PSG), and are influenced by technical design choices, user experience, and the setting in which the system is used [N1-F1][N5-F4][N2-F2][N3-F3].

### 1) How the three dimensions are evaluated and measured

Wearability, usability, and obtrusiveness are evaluated using a mix of **user-reported experience** and **objective performance metrics**. The branch reports consistently identify **comfort**, **ease of use**, **setup time**, **signal quality**, **artifact incidence**, **inter-scoring reliability**, and **sleep staging accuracy** as the main quantitative metrics reported in the literature [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1][N5-F4][N2-F2]. In other words, a wearable EEG system is judged not only by how well it records EEG, but also by how easy it is to apply, how comfortable it is to wear, and how much it interferes with normal behavior.

Obtrusiveness is measured or inferred through a combination of **user feedback**, **task completion**, and **physiological responses**. The evidence shows that **user-reported comfort and ease of use** are direct indicators of obtrusiveness, while **signal quality and artifact incidence** are indirect indicators because they reflect the system’s ability to function reliably without disrupting the recording [N5-F4][N2-F2]. The branch reports also note that obtrusiveness is strongly tied to the **lab versus home environment**: PSG is described as uncomfortable and having a negative impact on sleep, with the “first night effect” reducing total sleep time, sleep efficiency, and REM sleep [N5-F4]. This means obtrusiveness is not only a design feature but also a contextual experience that changes over repeated use and across settings [N5-F4].

### 2) What study designs and comparison groups are used across systems

The comparison methods used across systems are increasingly **standardized**, but they also vary by study objective and device family. The branch reports highlight several common designs:

- **Direct head-to-head comparisons** between electrode types, such as dry versus wet EEG electrodes, and between different wearable device families, such as ear-EEG and PSG [N2-F2][N5-F4].
- **Repeated-use or longitudinal studies** that measure changes over nights, such as the generic ear-EEG study comparing two nights with PSG and 10 nights with only ear-EEG [N5-F4].
- **Meta-analytic or pooled study designs** that compare many validation studies against PSG and analyze the influence of study design and device characteristics [N1-F1].
- **Paired or matched designs** that control for individual differences, such as the ear-EEG study comparing individualized earpieces with generic earpieces and finding that the subject effect was significant while the equipment effect was not [N5-F4].

These designs matter because wearability, usability, and obtrusiveness are not only assessed at a single point in time but also over repeated use and across different user populations [N5-F4][N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence also suggests that **comparison groups are often chosen to anchor performance relative to a reference system**, with PSG serving as the gold standard in many comparisons [N5-F4][N1-F1].

### 3) Which wearable EEG systems are most often compared and how they differ

The most often compared wearable EEG systems in the branch reports are **dry-electrode headbands, caps, adhesive patches, and ear-EEG systems**, with **ear-EEG** especially prominent as a less obtrusive alternative to PSG [N2-F2][N5-F4][N3-F3]. The evidence also implies that **caps and adhesive patches** are part of the broader family of wearable EEG systems being compared, even though they are not as explicitly detailed in the provided material [N3-F3][N5-F4].

Across these systems, the branch reports indicate that **dry-electrode systems** generally score better on **wearability and usability** because they are less reliant on conductive gel, easier to apply, and reusable [N2-F2][N5-F4]. However, they may score worse on **signal quality** in some short-term settings due to higher noise or contact impedance, and the evidence specifically notes that **sweat artifacts were more common in flat-type dry electrodes** [N2-F2][N5-R3]. In contrast, **ear-EEG systems** appear to score better on **wearability and obtrusiveness** because they are placed in or around the ear, reducing the need for headband or cap placement and improving comfort over repeated use [N5-F4]. The same study reports that users found the system easy to use and that comfort improved in repeated use [N5-F4].

PSG is not a wearable system in the same sense, but it remains important as the **reference system** against which wearable EEG systems are compared. The branch reports describe PSG as highly uncomfortable and impractical for everyday use outside the sleep laboratory, with the “first night effect” and reduced sleep quality in unfamiliar settings [N5-F4]. This makes PSG a useful benchmark for obtrusiveness, usability, and signal quality, but it is less suitable for evaluating wearability in real-world settings [N5-F4].

### 4) Why systems score differently on the three dimensions

The differences across systems are driven by **technical constraints** and **design choices**. The branch reports identify several key factors:
